corpus_definition: Something very silly or impossible to believe.

forms.definition: unkind laughter or words that make someone look silly
forms.example: He faced ridicule from his classmates because of his strange hat.

syn.note: Very close: laughing at someone in an unkind way.
Related: a strong feeling that someone is not worth respect.
Laughter is general and can be kind; ridicule is always unkind.

ant.note: Respect is a good opinion of someone, the opposite of laughing at them.
Praise means saying good things about someone.

forms.definition: the quality of being very silly and hard to believe
forms.example: Everyone laughed at the ridiculousness of the situation.

syn.note: Very close, a little more formal.
Easier word; silliness can be friendly and funny.

forms.definition: to laugh at someone or something in an unkind way
forms.example: They ridiculed his plan at first, but it worked.

syn.note: Very close: laugh at someone and copy them unkindly.
Everyday phrase with the same meaning.
Easy phrase; ridicule is stronger and more formal.
Teasing is often friendly; ridiculing is unkind.

ant.note: To say good things about someone.
To have a good opinion of someone and treat them well.

forms.definition: so silly or unreasonable that people want to laugh
forms.example: That excuse sounds completely ridiculous to me.

syn.note: Easy word; silly is softer and can be friendly.
Very close, a little more formal.
Very close, a stronger and less common word.
Informal: 'That's a crazy idea!'
Related: not fair or sensible, but not always funny.

ant.note: Reasonable means fair and easy to accept.

forms.definition: in a very silly way; also used to mean 'much too' or 'extremely'
forms.example: The tickets were ridiculously expensive.
forms.note: Most often used before adjectives: ridiculously cheap, ridiculously easy.

syn.note: Very close, a little more formal.
Extremely just means 'very very'; ridiculously adds that it is silly or hard to believe.

ant.note: Reasonably means to a fair, acceptable degree: reasonably cheap.

context.text: My brother wore a ridiculous hat to a wedding in Samarkand. Some cousins ridiculed him, but he just laughed. The hat was ridiculously big, but he loved it.

reviewer_note: Two rows with the same meaning merged (B1). Ridicule is the source noun and verb (ridiculous is made from it), so both are existing forms.

corpus_definition: To break or pull something apart quickly.

forms.definition: a long hole in cloth or paper where it was pulled apart
forms.example: There is a rip in the sleeve of my jacket.

syn.note: Very close and common. Careful: this tear rhymes with 'hair', not 'here'.
Easy, general word; a rip is usually long and made by pulling.
A split is a long crack or opening, often along a line.

forms.definition: to pull something apart quickly and with force
forms.example: Be careful not to rip your paper.

syn.note: Very close; rip is quicker and stronger.
To break into two parts, often along a line.
To cut or tear into many very small pieces.

ant.note: To repair a hole in clothes, often by sewing.

forms.definition: torn, with long holes in it
forms.example: He wore ripped jeans to the party.

syn.note: Very close and common.
Old and torn in many places.

context.text: Timur loves his ripped jeans, but his grandmother thinks they are just old. Yesterday he caught them on a fence, and now the rip is too big to wear.

reviewer_note: Noun rip is a same-spelling conversion; rip off / rip up are phrasal verbs and the informal 'ripped' (very muscular) is left out of the forms.

corpus_definition: To destroy a sheet of paper by pulling it into many small pieces.
particle_note: Separable: 'rip up the letter' or 'rip the letter up'. With a pronoun the particle goes after it: 'rip it up'.

relations.note: Very close and very common: 'She tore up the photo.'
To cut or tear into very thin pieces, often with a machine.
General word: to damage something so it cannot be used.

context.text: Aziz ripped up the old letter and threw the pieces away. Don't rip up your receipts; you may need them later.

reviewer_note: Phrasal verb; no forms. No true antonym listed.

corpus_definition: When fruit is ready to be eaten.

forms.definition: the state of fruit being fully grown and ready to eat
forms.example: You can check the ripeness of a melon by smelling it.

syn.note: Formal word for being fully grown or developed.

forms.definition: to become fully grown and ready to eat
forms.example: Apricots ripen in June in the Fergana Valley.

syn.note: More general: to become fully grown or developed.
General word for growing or changing over time.

forms.definition: fully grown and ready to be eaten
forms.example: The red apple is very sweet and ripe.

syn.note: Easy word: 'The tomatoes are ready to pick.'
More formal; also used for cheese and wine.

ant.note: Used for fruit that is not ready yet: 'These bananas are still green.'

context.text: Melons ripen in the hot sun of Khorezm in August. When they are ripe, the whole market smells sweet.

reviewer_note: Unripe kept as an antonym, not a form. Ripen uses the -en verb ending (not in the affix table), so no affix is claimed for it.

corpus_definition: The possibility of something bad happening.

forms.definition: the chance that something bad or dangerous may happen
forms.example: There is a small risk of rain today.

syn.note: Easy word; danger is the bad thing itself, a risk is the chance of it.
Something that can cause harm, often used in safety signs.
Something that may cause harm in the future.
Neutral: a chance can be good or bad; a risk is always bad.

ant.note: Safety is being free from danger.

forms.definition: to do something that could cause a bad result or loss
forms.example: He risked his life to save the child from the river.
forms.note: Often risk + -ing: 'Don't risk losing your job.'

syn.note: To put someone or something in danger; a little formal.
To take a chance hoping for a good result.
To be brave enough to do something difficult.

ant.note: To keep something safe from harm.

forms.definition: possibly dangerous or likely to end badly
forms.example: Driving fast in the rain is very risky.

syn.note: Easy and common; dangerous is often stronger.
Not safe; very close in everyday English.
Formal, used for work and health dangers.

forms.note: No common adverb in this family; riskily exists but is very rare.

context.text: Crossing the road without looking is risky. There is a real risk of an accident, so don't risk it just to save a minute.

reviewer_note: Noun and verb are same-spelling conversions; risk-taker is a compound and left out.

corpus_definition: a person who competes against another person

forms.definition: a person or team that tries to win against another
forms.example: He trained hard to beat his closest rival.

syn.note: Very close; also used for companies.
The person you play against in one game or fight.
Much stronger: an enemy hates you or wants to hurt you.

ant.note: Someone who helps and supports you.
Someone who works with you, not against you.

forms.definition: a situation where people or groups keep competing with each other
forms.example: There is a strong rivalry between the two football clubs.

syn.note: More general; rivalry is often long and strong.

forms.definition: to be as good or as important as someone or something else
forms.example: Few cities can rival Samarkand for beauty.

syn.note: To be equal to something in quality.
To be the same in size, number or quality.
To try to be better than others.

forms.note: No adjective in this family. In 'rival teams' or 'a rival company', rival is a noun used before another noun.

context.text: Pakhtakor and their old rival play in Tashkent this Saturday. The rivalry between the two clubs is famous, and few matches can rival it for noise.

reviewer_note: Person-noun headword stays the main noun entry; rivalry is an extra noun. Rival before nouns is attributive noun use, so the adjective slot is no_form.

corpus_definition: a long loose piece of clothing, like a dressing gown or coat

forms.definition: a long loose piece of clothing, worn at home or for special events
forms.example: The judge entered the courtroom wearing a long black robe.

syn.note: A long dress or a long official piece of clothing.
British: a robe you wear at home over your night clothes.
A soft robe you wear after a bath; common in American English.
A long coat with no sleeves that hangs from the shoulders.

forms.definition: to dress someone in long loose formal clothes
forms.example: The judges were robed in black.
forms.note: Mostly used in the passive: be robed in.

syn.note: Easy and general.
Formal word for giving or putting on clothes.

forms.definition: wearing a long loose piece of formal clothing
forms.example: The robed musicians played all night.

syn.note: General: wearing clothes.

context.text: My grandfather wore a long blue robe called a chapan at the wedding in Bukhara. Next to him, the robed musicians played until morning.

reviewer_note: Wardrobe looks related but is a compound and is left out; robe verb and robed are formal.

corpus_definition: The function or part played by someone.

forms.definition: the job or part that someone has in a group or situation
forms.example: Everyone has an important role in the team.
forms.note: Also the character an actor plays in a film. Don't confuse with roll (bread, or to turn over).

syn.note: Easy and very close: 'play a part / play a role'.
More formal; often used for things as well as people.
Easy word for the work someone must do.
A place or job in an organization.
Something you must do because it is your job.

context.text: In our class project, every student had a role. My role was to find pictures, and Malika wrote the text.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; role model and role-play are compounds and left out; roll is a different word.

corpus_definition: Related to love or deep feelings of affection.

forms.definition: a loving relationship between two people, often a short one
forms.example: Their romance started at university in Tashkent.

syn.note: A relationship between two people in love, often secret or short.
General word for two people who are together.
The feeling itself; romance is the relationship or the mood.

forms.definition: a style of art and writing from about 1800 that shows strong feelings and nature
forms.example: We studied romanticism in our literature class.
forms.note: Belongs to romantic = the art and writing style (the Romantic poets), not love between people.

forms.definition: to show something as better or more exciting than it really is
forms.example: Films often romanticize life in big cities.
forms.note: Belongs to romantic = seeing things in a beautiful but unreal way, not love between people. British spelling: romanticise.

forms.definition: connected with love and deep, warm feelings for someone
forms.example: They had a romantic dinner by the sea.
forms.note: Also a noun for a person who believes in love and beauty: 'He is a real romantic.'

syn.note: Showing love and care, also for family and friends.
Gentle and loving.
Having very strong feelings, including love.
Showing soft feelings, sometimes too much.

ant.note: Not showing love or warm feelings; practical.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with love between two people
forms.example: They are not romantically involved; they are just friends.

syn.note: In a way that shows love or care.
In a gentle, loving way.

context.text: Dilnoza and Bekzod had a romantic dinner in a small cafe in Tashkent. Their romance started at university, and he still behaves very romantically.

reviewer_note: Romanticism and romanticize belong to the art/idealizing sense, so they are other_meaning; no transparent affix split (romant- is not a word), so affixes are empty.

corpus_definition: to slowly decay and break down in a bad way

forms.definition: the slow process of going soft and bad, or the bad part itself
forms.example: There was rot in the old wooden floor.

syn.note: Very close; decay is a little more formal.
A soft green or grey growth on old food. American spelling: mold.

forms.definition: to slowly go soft and bad because of age or water
forms.example: The old wood began to rot in the rain.

syn.note: Very close; decay is a little more formal.
Easy phrase, used for food: 'The milk went bad.'
Scientific word for breaking down naturally.
Used for food that is no longer good to eat.

forms.definition: gone soft and bad, so it cannot be eaten or used
forms.example: Throw away the rotten tomatoes.
forms.note: Informally it also means 'very bad': rotten weather.

syn.note: Easy word: 'This egg is bad.'
More formal, often for wood or teeth.
Used for food. British also: spoilt.

ant.note: Fresh food is new and good to eat.

forms.definition: slowly going soft and bad at this moment
forms.example: The smell of rotting fruit filled the market.

syn.note: Very close, a little more formal.

forms.note: No adverb in this family in this meaning.

context.text: Don't leave the apples in a plastic bag, or they will rot. Last week I found three rotten ones at the bottom of the bag.

reviewer_note: Rotten is the old participle used as the main adjective; rotting is an extra participial adjective.
